prompt.context: Your client, the owner of Cut-N-Edge, a successful chain of hair salons in a large metropolitan area, believes there is opportunity to grow her business by adding manicure services to her existing salons. Currently the salons offer only premium haircut and styling services. The salons are staffed by trained hair stylists.
prompt.question: Your client wants help understanding whether expanding into manicures is a good idea and, if she were to pursue the expansion, what kind of customer volumes she should prepare for in the first year.

clarifying_info.a: Primary objective is short-term profitability — must be profitable at the end of year one to go forward with expansion.

clarifying_info.q: Will the client add space to the salons?
clarifying_info.a: No. The owner will not add space to existing salons; instead she will swap out haircut stations for manicure stations.

clarifying_info.q: How does the nail salon business perform in a downturn?
clarifying_info.a: Hair salons are relatively recession-proof. Nail salons see revenue decline in a bad economy but have high margins to buoy them through tough times.
The majority of the salon's current customers are adult women.

clarifying_info.q: What are the salon's operating hours?
clarifying_info.a: The salon is open five days per week, Tuesday through Saturday.

framework: Will manicure stations be more profitable than haircut stations by end of year 1? Compare revenues and costs across both service types.

Is this an attractive complementary market long-term? Consider: (a) market size and growth rate of metro manicure market, (b) existing customer demand and willingness to pay, (c) impact on Cut-N-Edge brand and future growth options.
What customer volumes might the manicure service attract? Split into: existing customers who add manicures, and new customers attracted by the new service.
Revenue drivers: types of services (gel, French, regular manicure), product sales (lotion, polish), associated services (massage, paraffin wax).
Cost drivers: labor, materials (polish, dryers, tools, lotion, towels), SG&A, investment cost of station conversion.

questions.prompt: Why might the salon consider this expansion in the first place? Brainstorm possible reasons.
questions.guidance: Capture existing customers who already get manicures elsewhere. Attract new customers for nail services who might also try salon services. Build brand beyond haircut/styling and create a platform for further expansion (facials, waxing, pedicures, massage). Increase utilization of existing space and capacity.

questions.prompt:
Your client estimates she can replace four haircut stations with six manicure stations in each salon. The investment is $5,000 per salon. Using the data below, calculate the difference in daily profitability between the four haircut stations and the six manicure stations.

Haircut: 4 stations, 50% utilization, 60-min appointments, $50 avg price, $35 unit cost.
Manicure: 6 stations, 80% utilization, 45-min appointments, $20 avg price, $10 unit cost.
questions.guidance: A strong answer works through stations → daily appointments → revenue → cost → profit for each service type, then computes the incremental profit and payback period. The candidate should note that the $5,000 investment is recouped in about 21 days, and flag that the analysis assumes haircut volume is fully displaced (some could shift to remaining stations).

math.setup: Calculate daily appointments per service type: (# stations) × (utilization) × (operating minutes per day / appointment duration). Use 8-hour operating day = 480 minutes. Then multiply by price and cost per appointment.
steps: Haircut daily appts: 4 stations × 50% utilization × (480 min / 60 min) = 4 × 0.5 × 8 = 16 appts
Manicure daily appts: 6 stations × 80% utilization × (480 min / 45 min) = 6 × 0.8 × ~10.67 ≈ 48 appts (casebook rounds to 48)
Incremental daily profit (manicure minus haircut): $480 - $240 = $240 per salon per day
math.answer: Adding manicure stations yields an incremental $240 in profit per salon per day. The $5,000 investment is recouped in approximately 21 days.

questions.prompt:
Calculate the total number of manicure appointments the client could expect in year one. The client anticipates two customer segments: (a) existing haircut customers who add a manicure, and (b) new customers attracted by the new service.

Existing customers: 25 salons, approximately 1,500 regular customers per salon (note: casebook states 500 regular customers — use whichever figure the interviewer provides), visiting once every 10 weeks (~5 times per year), 20% likely to add a manicure.

New customers: For every $100 spent on advertising, 15 new customers are acquired. Year-1 advertising budget is $15,000.
questions.guidance: A strong answer sets up the two-segment model cleanly, applies the given assumptions, and arrives at roughly 39,750 total appointments. The candidate should acknowledge the assumptions (opt-in rate, advertising efficiency) and note uncertainty.

math.setup: Segment 1: salons × customers per salon × opt-in rate × visits per year. Segment 2: (advertising budget / $100) × 15 new customers.
steps: Segment 1 (existing customers): 25 salons × 1,500 customers × 20% opt-in × 5 visits/year = 37,500 appointments
math.answer: Cut-N-Edge could anticipate approximately 39,750 manicure appointments in year one.

brainstorming.prompt: Why might the salon owner consider adding manicure services in the first place?

categories.name: Existing Customer Capture
ideas: Retain existing customers who currently get manicures at competitor salons
Increase share of wallet per customer visit
Provide a one-stop-shop experience for female customers

categories.name: New Customer Acquisition
ideas: Attract new customers seeking nail services who may then trial haircut services
Expand brand awareness in a complementary category

categories.name: Brand and Growth Platform
ideas: Build the Cut-N-Edge brand beyond haircuts and styling
Create a foundation for further personal-care expansion: facials, waxing, pedicures, massage

categories.name: Operational Efficiency
ideas: Increase utilization of existing floor space
Smooth appointment scheduling by offering alternative services
Leverage existing SG&A base across a broader revenue stream

recommendation: Proceed with adding manicure stations across the Cut-N-Edge salon network. The conversion yields an incremental $240 in profit per salon per day and recoups the $5,000 per-salon investment in approximately 21 days.
The client can expect approximately 39,750 manicure appointments in year one, driven primarily by existing customers adding manicures to their haircut visits.
risks: Opt-in rate among existing customers (assumed 20%) may be optimistic; actual demand is unvalidated.
Displacing haircut stations reduces haircut capacity; assumes displaced haircut volume can shift to remaining stations.
Manicure staffing requires recruiting and training nail technicians, which may take time and increase labor costs.
Brand risk if manicure quality does not meet the premium standard Cut-N-Edge is known for.
Advertising-driven new customer acquisition (15 customers per $100) is an estimate that may not hold at scale.
next_steps: Conduct a gradual rollout across the salon network (pilot one or two locations) to validate opt-in rates and profitability before full deployment.
Survey existing customers to better estimate demand and willingness to pay for manicure services.
Conduct a pricing exercise to optimize the $20 price point and expected revenue per appointment.
Begin recruiting and interviewing licensed nail technicians to staff the new stations.
